# Edward Hirsch

[http://www.edwardhirsch.com/](http://www.edwardhirsch.com/)

B.1950

Share

![Image 6: Image of Edward Hirsch](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=2292,h=1500,q=80/content/images/32b1ccbcf6549907ab3284dc05f86729d274b2eb.jpeg)

Photo by Julie Dermansky

Poet and author Edward Hirsch has built a reputation as an attentive and elegant writer and reader of poetry. Over the course of many collections of poetry and criticism, and the long-running “Poet’s Choice” column in the _Washington Post_,Hirsch has transformed the quotidian into poetry in his own work, as well as demonstrated his adeptness at explicating the nuances and shades of feeling, tradition, and craft at work in the poetry of others. Introducing Hirsch at the National Arts Club, Pulitzer Prize-winning author [Jhumpa Lahiri](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/jhumpa-lahiri) remarked: “The trademarks of his poems are things I strive to bring to my own writing: to be intimate but restrained, to be tender without being sentimental, to witness life without flinching, and above all, to isolate and preserve those details of our existence so often overlooked, so easily forgotten, so essential to our souls.” “I would like to speak in my poems with what the Romantic poets called ‘the true voice of feeling,’” Hirsch told _Contemporary Authors._ “I believe, as [Ezra Pound](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/ezra-pound)once said, that when it comes to poetry, ‘only emotion endures.’”

Described by Peter Stitt in _Poetry_ as “a poet of genuine talent and feeling,” Hirsch was nominated for the National Book Critics Circle Award for his first volume, _For the Sleepwalkers_ (1981); his second, _Wild Gratitude_(1986) won the award in 1987. He has been awarded fellowships from the National Endowment for the Arts, the Guggenheim Foundation, and received a MacArthur “Genius Grant” in 1997. His numerous other awards include an Ingram Merrill Foundation Award, the Rome Prize from the American Academy in Rome, and a Lila Wallace-Reader’s Digest Writers’ Award. A former professor at Wayne State University and the University of Houston, Hirsch is president of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation and is a Chancellor of the Academy of American Poets.

Born in 1950 in Chicago, Hirsch was educated at Grinnell College and the University of Pennsylvania, where he earned a PhD in folklore. His first books contain vignettes of urban life and numerous tributes to artists, which, according to [David Wojahn](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/david-wojahn) in the _New York Times Book Review_ _,_ “begin as troubled meditations on human suffering [but] end in celebration.” _New Republic_ contributor Jay Parini wrote that in _For the Sleepwalkers_ _,_ “Hirsch inhabits, poem by poem, dozens of other skins. He can become Rimbaud, Rilke, Paul Klee, or Matisse, in each case convincingly.” Hirsch uses other voices in later works like _On Love_(1998)_._ Taking on the personae of dozens of poets from the past, including diverse writers like [D.H. Lawrence](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/archive/poet.html?id=3959), [Charles Baudelaire](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/charles-baudelaire), and Jimi Hendrix, Hirsch creates an imaginary conversation between them as they discuss the subject of love.

Hirsch’s interest in mining the past and traditions of poetry extends to his critical work as well. _How to Read a Poem and Fall in Love with Poetry_(1999) presents close-readings of an eclectic mix of poems and poets, written in an accessible style. _The Demon and the Angel: Searching for the Source of Artistic Inspiration_ (2003) considers the concept of _duende,_ which posits that artistic creation arises out of a heightened state, or power. Hirsch explores the implications of _duende—_ made most famous by[Federico García Lorca](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/federico-garcia-lorca)—across a variety of artists, including Martha Graham and Lorca himself. Hirsch’s encyclopedic knowledge of poetry, poets, and poetics served him during his tenure at the _Washington Post_,where he penned the weekly “Poet’s Choice” column. Collecting the columns into the book _Poet’s Choice_(2006), Hirsch stated his goals for his work as a critic: “I write for both initiated and uninitiated readers of poetry. I like to spread the word ... My notion was to make links and connections, to bring forward unknown poets, and to help people to think about poetry in a somewhat deeper way. It seemed to work.” In 2014, Hirsch published _A Poet’s Glossary_, a comprehensive look at poetry’s forms, devices, groups, movements, -isms, aesthetics, rhetorical terms, and folklore.

Hirsch’s more recent volumes of poetry include _Earthly Measures_(1994), _On Love_(1998), and _Lay Back the Darkness_(2003), which includes treatments of the Orpheus myth as well as several ekphrasis poems. _The Living Fire: New and Selected Poems 1972–2010_ shows, according to [Peter Campion](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/peter-campion) in the _New York Times_, “a kind of model for the growth of poetic intelligence.” Campion went on to note, “What makes Hirsch so singular in American poetry is the balance he strikes between the quotidian and something completely other—an irrational counterforce.” Though noting that Hirsch’s poems sometimes sink to rhetoric, Campion concluded that, “Hirsch situates himself between the ordinary and the ecstatic. The everyday and the otherworldly temper each other in these excellent ­poems, and American poetry gains new strength as a result.”

Hirsch’s poetry collection _Gabriel_ (2014), which explores the death of his son, was longlisted for the National Book Award.[Eavan Boland](https://poetryfoundation.org/bio/eavan-boland)described _Gabriel_ as “a masterpiece of sorrow ... the creation of the loved and lost boy is one of the poem’s most important effects.”

Hirsch lives in Brooklyn.

# Edward Hirsch

[http://www.edwardhirsch.com/](http://www.edwardhirsch.com/)

B.1950

Share

![Image 6: Image of Edward Hirsch](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=2292,h=1500,q=80/content/images/32b1ccbcf6549907ab3284dc05f86729d274b2eb.jpeg)

Photo by Julie Dermansky

Poet and author Edward Hirsch has built a reputation as an attentive and elegant writer and reader of poetry. Over the course of many collections of poetry and criticism, and the long-running “Poet’s Choice” column in the _Washington Post_,Hirsch has transformed the quotidian into poetry in his own work, as well as demonstrated his adeptness at explicating the nuances and shades of feeling, tradition, and craft at work in the poetry of others. Introducing Hirsch at the National Arts Club, Pulitzer Prize-winning author [Jhumpa Lahiri](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/jhumpa-lahiri) remarked: “The trademarks of his poems are things I strive to bring to my own writing: to be intimate but restrained, to be tender without being sentimental, to witness life without flinching, and above all, to isolate and preserve those details of our existence so often overlooked, so easily forgotten, so essential to our souls.” “I would like to speak in my poems with what the Romantic poets called ‘the true voice of feeling,’” Hirsch told _Contemporary Authors._ “I believe, as [Ezra Pound](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/ezra-pound)once said, that when it comes to poetry, ‘only emotion endures.’”

Described by Peter Stitt in _Poetry_ as “a poet of genuine talent and feeling,” Hirsch was nominated for the National Book Critics Circle Award for his first volume, _For the Sleepwalkers_ (1981); his second, _Wild Gratitude_(1986) won the award in 1987. He has been awarded fellowships from the National Endowment for the Arts, the Guggenheim Foundation, and received a MacArthur “Genius Grant” in 1997. His numerous other awards include an Ingram Merrill Foundation Award, the Rome Prize from the American Academy in Rome, and a Lila Wallace-Reader’s Digest Writers’ Award. A former professor at Wayne State University and the University of Houston, Hirsch is president of the John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation and is a Chancellor of the Academy of American Poets.

Born in 1950 in Chicago, Hirsch was educated at Grinnell College and the University of Pennsylvania, where he earned a PhD in folklore. His first books contain vignettes of urban life and numerous tributes to artists, which, according to [David Wojahn](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/david-wojahn) in the _New York Times Book Review_ _,_ “begin as troubled meditations on human suffering [but] end in celebration.” _New Republic_ contributor Jay Parini wrote that in _For the Sleepwalkers_ _,_ “Hirsch inhabits, poem by poem, dozens of other skins. He can become Rimbaud, Rilke, Paul Klee, or Matisse, in each case convincingly.” Hirsch uses other voices in later works like _On Love_(1998)_._ Taking on the personae of dozens of poets from the past, including diverse writers like [D.H. Lawrence](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/archive/poet.html?id=3959), [Charles Baudelaire](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/charles-baudelaire), and Jimi Hendrix, Hirsch creates an imaginary conversation between them as they discuss the subject of love.

Hirsch’s interest in mining the past and traditions of poetry extends to his critical work as well. _How to Read a Poem and Fall in Love with Poetry_(1999) presents close-readings of an eclectic mix of poems and poets, written in an accessible style. _The Demon and the Angel: Searching for the Source of Artistic Inspiration_ (2003) considers the concept of _duende,_ which posits that artistic creation arises out of a heightened state, or power. Hirsch explores the implications of _duende—_ made most famous by[Federico García Lorca](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/federico-garcia-lorca)—across a variety of artists, including Martha Graham and Lorca himself. Hirsch’s encyclopedic knowledge of poetry, poets, and poetics served him during his tenure at the _Washington Post_,where he penned the weekly “Poet’s Choice” column. Collecting the columns into the book _Poet’s Choice_(2006), Hirsch stated his goals for his work as a critic: “I write for both initiated and uninitiated readers of poetry. I like to spread the word ... My notion was to make links and connections, to bring forward unknown poets, and to help people to think about poetry in a somewhat deeper way. It seemed to work.” In 2014, Hirsch published _A Poet’s Glossary_, a comprehensive look at poetry’s forms, devices, groups, movements, -isms, aesthetics, rhetorical terms, and folklore.

Hirsch’s more recent volumes of poetry include _Earthly Measures_(1994), _On Love_(1998), and _Lay Back the Darkness_(2003), which includes treatments of the Orpheus myth as well as several ekphrasis poems. _The Living Fire: New and Selected Poems 1972–2010_ shows, according to [Peter Campion](http://www.poetryfoundation.org/bio/peter-campion) in the _New York Times_, “a kind of model for the growth of poetic intelligence.” Campion went on to note, “What makes Hirsch so singular in American poetry is the balance he strikes between the quotidian and something completely other—an irrational counterforce.” Though noting that Hirsch’s poems sometimes sink to rhetoric, Campion concluded that, “Hirsch situates himself between the ordinary and the ecstatic. The everyday and the otherworldly temper each other in these excellent ­poems, and American poetry gains new strength as a result.”

Hirsch’s poetry collection _Gabriel_ (2014), which explores the death of his son, was longlisted for the National Book Award.[Eavan Boland](https://poetryfoundation.org/bio/eavan-boland)described _Gabriel_ as “a masterpiece of sorrow ... the creation of the loved and lost boy is one of the poem’s most important effects.”

Hirsch lives in Brooklyn.

# Pegasus Poetry Book Prize

Share

The Pegasus Poetry Book Prize, established in 2025 in partnership with Graywolf Press, awards $10,000 and publication to an unpublished first or second poetry collection by a United States poet 40 or older. The recipient will also receive a residency at Ragdale. This prize replaces the Poetry Foundation’s former [Emily Dickinson First Book Award](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/awards/past-awards) and will be offered periodically rather than annually.

2026 Pegasus Poetry Book Prize Recipient

*   ![Image 6: meg-day](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=10,h=10,q=50,blur=3/content/images/pol/2021-08/meg-day.jpeg)2026 Sound Lasso By Meg Day  [Meg Day](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/meg-day)’s second full-length collection, _Sound Lasso_, captures the many ways we can “sing without a sound.” In Day’s poems, desires of the mind and body echo with divine potential. The book traces absent lovers through a series of [aubades](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/education/glossary/aubade), reconceives the self in various portraits, and offers Deaf [erasures](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/education/glossary/erasure-poetry) that suggest the inaudible can be both blessing and comfort as we find new ways of speaking. This lush, searching book reminds us that naming—ourselves, each other, and our various hungers—can be a powerful improvisation, akin to godliness.

–Lindsay Garbutt, deputy editor, _Poetry_

_Sound Lasso_ will be published by Graywolf Press in 2028.

**Finalist**

The 2026 finalist for the Pegasus Poetry Book Prize was _The Far Edge of the Wound Is a Field,_ a manuscript by[Paul Hlava Ceballos](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/paul-hlava-ceballos).

## Emily Dickinson First Book Award

The Emily Dickinson First Book Award is designed to recognize an American poet of at least 40 years of age who has yet to publish a first collection of poetry. The Randall Jarrell Award in Criticism recognized poetry criticism aimed at a large general readership rather than an audience of specialists.

## Mark Twain Poetry Award

The Mark Twain Poetry Award of $25,000 recognized a poet’s contributions to humor in American poetry.

## Neglected Masters Award

The Neglected Masters Award of $50,000 brought to the reading public renewed critical attention to the work of an under-recognized yet significant American poet. If previously unpublished or no longer in print, the works of Neglected Masters were published in collaboration with the Library of America.

## Verse Drama Prize

The Verse Drama Prize honored a living poet who had written a previously unpublished, outstanding original verse drama in English. The award recipient received a cash prize of $10,000 and a staged reading of the winning manuscript in Chicago.

**Milkweed Editions** is an independent nonprofit literary publisher that originated from the _**Milkweed Chronicle**_ literary and arts journal established in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") in 1979. The journal ceased and the business transitioned to publishing. It releases eighteen to twenty new books each year in the genres of fiction, nonfiction, and poetry. Milkweed Editions annually awards three prizes for poetry: the Lindquist & Vennum Prize for Poetry,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-:0-1) the Jake Adam York Prize (in collaboration with _Copper Nickel_), and they are a partner publisher for the National Poetry Series. In 2016, Milkweed Editions opened an [independent bookstore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_bookstore "Independent bookstore").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-:1-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Milkweed_Editions&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

_Milkweed Chronicle_ was co-founded in 1979 as a literature and art journal by [Emilie Buchwald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilie_Buchwald "Emilie Buchwald") and R.W. Scholes in Minneapolis. _Milkweed Chronicle'_ s first issue was published in 1980. Buchwald served as editor and Scholes as [art director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_director "Art director"). The journal ran for 21 issues until 1987. It featured local and national writers and artists.

In the mid-1980s, the publication ceased and the business transitioned to publishing. Milkweed Editions published its first book and ceased publication of the journal.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-3) Since this first publication, the press has published more than three hundred and fifty titles.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-4)

In 1999, Milkweed combined forces with [Minnesota Center for Book Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Center_for_Book_Arts "Minnesota Center for Book Arts") and the [Loft Literary Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_Literary_Center "Loft Literary Center") to purchase an old warehouse in downtown Minneapolis to house each organization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-5) They named the warehouse the [Open Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Book_Minneapolis "Open Book Minneapolis").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-6)

In 2007, Daniel Slager was named Publisher & CEO of Milkweed Editions. Since his arrival, Slager has focused the press on the publication of fiction, nonfiction, and poetry, and has focused on publishing more work in translation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-7) In 2016, the press opened a bookstore, Milkweed Books.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-:1-2)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-10)

## Milkweed Prizes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Milkweed_Editions&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Milkweed Prizes")]

The **Lindquist & Vennum Prize for Poetry** was established in 2011 by Milkweed Editions and the [Lindquist & Vennum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum "Lindquist & Vennum") Foundation.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-11) Submissions for this regional prize are accepted only from poets residing in the states of the Upper Midwest. The winner receives a $10,000 cash prize and a publishing contract.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-:0-1)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-12) Previous winners have included Patricia Kirkpatrick,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-13) Rebecca Dunham,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-14) Michael Bazzett,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-15) Jennifer Willoughby,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-16) and Chris Santiago.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-17)

In 2017, Milkweed Editions announced the [Max Ritvo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ritvo "Max Ritvo") Poetry Prize, a US$10,000 award supported by the [Alan B. Slifka Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_B._Slifka_Foundation "Alan B. Slifka Foundation").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-18) Grady Chambers was the Inaugural winner award of this prize, announced December 2017.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-19)

## Awards and media recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Milkweed_Editions&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Awards and media recognition")]

Milkweed Editions was the 2021 winner of the [AWP Small Press Publisher Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_AWP_Small_Press_Publisher_Award "List of winners of the AWP Small Press Publisher Award") given by the [Association of Writers & Writing Programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Writers_&_Writing_Programs#Small_Press_Publisher_Award "Association of Writers & Writing Programs") which "acknowledges the hard work, creativity, and innovation of these presses and journals, and honors their contributions to the literary landscape through their publication of consistently excellent work."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-21) The press has been further recognized by media attention in interviews and features, including [Literary Hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_Hub "Literary Hub")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-22) and _[Publishers Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers\_Weekly "Publishers Weekly")_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-24)

**Milkweed Editions** is an independent nonprofit literary publisher that originated from the _**Milkweed Chronicle**_ literary and arts journal established in [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis") in 1979. The journal ceased and the business transitioned to publishing. It releases eighteen to twenty new books each year in the genres of fiction, nonfiction, and poetry. Milkweed Editions annually awards three prizes for poetry: the Lindquist & Vennum Prize for Poetry,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-:0-1) the Jake Adam York Prize (in collaboration with _Copper Nickel_), and they are a partner publisher for the National Poetry Series. In 2016, Milkweed Editions opened an [independent bookstore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_bookstore "Independent bookstore").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-:1-2)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Milkweed_Editions&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

_Milkweed Chronicle_ was co-founded in 1979 as a literature and art journal by [Emilie Buchwald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emilie_Buchwald "Emilie Buchwald") and R.W. Scholes in Minneapolis. _Milkweed Chronicle'_ s first issue was published in 1980. Buchwald served as editor and Scholes as [art director](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Art_director "Art director"). The journal ran for 21 issues until 1987. It featured local and national writers and artists.

In the mid-1980s, the publication ceased and the business transitioned to publishing. Milkweed Editions published its first book and ceased publication of the journal.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-3) Since this first publication, the press has published more than three hundred and fifty titles.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-4)

In 1999, Milkweed combined forces with [Minnesota Center for Book Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota_Center_for_Book_Arts "Minnesota Center for Book Arts") and the [Loft Literary Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loft_Literary_Center "Loft Literary Center") to purchase an old warehouse in downtown Minneapolis to house each organization.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-5) They named the warehouse the [Open Book](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Book_Minneapolis "Open Book Minneapolis").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-6)

In 2007, Daniel Slager was named Publisher & CEO of Milkweed Editions. Since his arrival, Slager has focused the press on the publication of fiction, nonfiction, and poetry, and has focused on publishing more work in translation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-7) In 2016, the press opened a bookstore, Milkweed Books.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-:1-2)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-10)

## Milkweed Prizes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Milkweed_Editions&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Milkweed Prizes")]

The **Lindquist & Vennum Prize for Poetry** was established in 2011 by Milkweed Editions and the [Lindquist & Vennum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum "Lindquist & Vennum") Foundation.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-11) Submissions for this regional prize are accepted only from poets residing in the states of the Upper Midwest. The winner receives a $10,000 cash prize and a publishing contract.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-:0-1)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-12) Previous winners have included Patricia Kirkpatrick,[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-13) Rebecca Dunham,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-14) Michael Bazzett,[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-15) Jennifer Willoughby,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-16) and Chris Santiago.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-17)

In 2017, Milkweed Editions announced the [Max Ritvo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ritvo "Max Ritvo") Poetry Prize, a US$10,000 award supported by the [Alan B. Slifka Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_B._Slifka_Foundation "Alan B. Slifka Foundation").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-18) Grady Chambers was the Inaugural winner award of this prize, announced December 2017.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-19)

## Awards and media recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Milkweed_Editions&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Awards and media recognition")]

Milkweed Editions was the 2021 winner of the [AWP Small Press Publisher Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_AWP_Small_Press_Publisher_Award "List of winners of the AWP Small Press Publisher Award") given by the [Association of Writers & Writing Programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Writers_&_Writing_Programs#Small_Press_Publisher_Award "Association of Writers & Writing Programs") which "acknowledges the hard work, creativity, and innovation of these presses and journals, and honors their contributions to the literary landscape through their publication of consistently excellent work."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-20)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-21) The press has been further recognized by media attention in interviews and features, including [Literary Hub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_Hub "Literary Hub")[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-22) and _[Publishers Weekly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishers\_Weekly "Publishers Weekly")_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milkweed_Editions#cite_note-24)

**Lindquist & Vennum LLP** was a law firm of approximately 170 attorneys that provided corporate finance, transactional and litigation services for clients from offices in [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), and [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota"). The firm was formed in 1968 when Lindquist, Magnuson & Glennon combined with Vennum, Newhall, Ackman & Goetz. As of January 1, 2018, the firm merged with and took the name of [Ballard Spahr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballard_Spahr "Ballard Spahr").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-5)

## Pro bono service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lindquist_%26_Vennum&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Pro bono service")]

Since 1997, Lindquist & Vennum has achieved 100 percent pro bono participation by its partners, associates and paralegals. In 2007, the firm was first to be honored for its pro bono efforts by the Minnesota Judicial Council, a newly formed policy-making body of the Minnesota Judicial Branch. In 2013, the firm was named to [The National Law Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Law_Journal "The National Law Journal")'s Pro Bono Hot List.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-6)

**Lindquist & Vennum LLP** was a law firm of approximately 170 attorneys that provided corporate finance, transactional and litigation services for clients from offices in [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), and [South Dakota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Dakota "South Dakota"). The firm was formed in 1968 when Lindquist, Magnuson & Glennon combined with Vennum, Newhall, Ackman & Goetz. As of January 1, 2018, the firm merged with and took the name of [Ballard Spahr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballard_Spahr "Ballard Spahr").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-5)

## Pro bono service

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Lindquist_%26_Vennum&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Pro bono service")]

Since 1997, Lindquist & Vennum has achieved 100 percent pro bono participation by its partners, associates and paralegals. In 2007, the firm was first to be honored for its pro bono efforts by the Minnesota Judicial Council, a newly formed policy-making body of the Minnesota Judicial Branch. In 2013, the firm was named to [The National Law Journal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_National_Law_Journal "The National Law Journal")'s Pro Bono Hot List.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindquist_&_Vennum#cite_note-6)

Not to be confused with [Ed Hirsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Hirsh "Ed Hirsh") or [E. D. Hirsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._D._Hirsch "E. D. Hirsch").

Edward Hirsch

**Edward M. Hirsch** (born January 20, 1950) is an American poet and critic who wrote a national [bestseller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bestseller "Bestseller") about reading poetry. He has published nine books of poems, including _The Living Fire: New and Selected Poems_ (2010), which brings together thirty-five years of work, and _Gabriel: A Poem_ (2014), a book-length elegy for his son that _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_ called "a masterpiece of sorrow." He has also published five prose books about poetry. He is president of the [John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Simon_Guggenheim_Memorial_Foundation "John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation") in New York City.

Hirsch was born in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"). He had a childhood involvement with poetry, which he later explored at [Grinnell College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grinnell_College "Grinnell College") and the [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), where he received a [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PhD "PhD") in folklore. He is Jewish.

Hirsch was a professor of English at [Wayne State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_State_University "Wayne State University"). In 1985, he joined the faculty at the [University of Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Houston "University of Houston"), where he spent 17 years as a professor in the Creative Writing Program and Department of English. He was appointed the fourth president of the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation on September 3, 2002. He holds seven honorary degrees.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Hirsch&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Hirsch is a well-known advocate for poetry whose essays have been published in the _American Poetry Review_, _The New York Times Book Review_, _[The New York Review of Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Review\_of\_Books "The New York Review of Books")_, and elsewhere. He wrote a weekly column on poetry for _The Washington Post Book World_ from 2002 to 2005, which resulted in his book _Poet’s Choice_ (2006). His other prose books include _Responsive Reading_ (1999), _The Demon and the Angel: Searching for the Source of Artistic Inspiration_ (2002), and _A Poet's Glossary_ (2014), a complete compendium of poetic terms. He is the editor of _Transforming Vision: Writers on Art_ (1994), _Theodore Roethke’s Selected Poems_ (2005) and _To a Nightingale_ (2007). He is the co-editor of _A William Maxwell Portrait: Memories and Appreciations_ and _The Making of a Sonnet: A Norton Anthology_ (2008). He also edits the series "The Writer’s World" (Trinity University Press).

Hirsch's first collection of poems, _For the Sleepwalkers_, received the Lavan Younger Poets Award from the Academy of American Poets[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hirsch#cite_note-1) and the Delmore Schwartz Memorial Award from New York University. His second book, _Wild Gratitude_, received the National Book Critics Circle Award in 1986. He was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hirsch#cite_note-pf-2) in 1985 and a five-year [MacArthur Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Fellowship "MacArthur Fellowship") in 1997. He received the [William Riley Parker Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Riley_Parker_Prize "William Riley Parker Prize") from the Modern Language Association for the best scholarly essay in _PMLA_ for the year 1991. He has also received an [Ingram Merrill Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingram_Merrill_Foundation "Ingram Merrill Foundation") Award, a National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship, the Rome Prize from the American Academy in Rome, a Pablo Neruda Presidential Medal of Honor, and the American Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Literature. He is a former Chancellor of the Academy of American Poets. A volume of his poetry, _Earthly Measures_, was selected by critic Harold Bloom for inclusion on his list of works defining the [Western Canon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Western_Canon "The Western Canon").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hirsch#cite_note-3) Hirsch's book _How to Read a Poem and Fall in Love with Poetry_ (1999) was a surprise bestseller and is widely taught throughout the country.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American poet and critic (born 1950)

Not to be confused with [Ed Hirsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Hirsh "Ed Hirsh") or [E. D. Hirsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._D._Hirsch "E. D. Hirsch").

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Edward_Hirsch_2.jpg/250px-Edward_Hirsch_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Edward_Hirsch_2.jpg)

Edward Hirsch

**Edward M. Hirsch** (born January 20, 1950) is an American poet and critic who wrote a national [bestseller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bestseller "Bestseller") about reading poetry. He has published nine books of poems, including _The Living Fire: New and Selected Poems_ (2010), which brings together thirty-five years of work, and _Gabriel: A Poem_ (2014), a book-length elegy for his son that _[The New Yorker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_Yorker "The New Yorker")_ called "a masterpiece of sorrow." He has also published five prose books about poetry. He is president of the [John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Simon_Guggenheim_Memorial_Foundation "John Simon Guggenheim Memorial Foundation") in New York City.

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Hirsch&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/b/b4/Ambox_important.svg/40px-Ambox_important.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)This section of a [biography of a living person](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Biographies_of_living_persons "Wikipedia:Biographies of living persons")**does not [include](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources") any [references or sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")**. Hirsch was born in [Chicago](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago "Chicago"). He had a childhood involvement with poetry, which he later explored at [Grinnell College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grinnell_College "Grinnell College") and the [University of Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Pennsylvania "University of Pennsylvania"), where he received a [PhD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PhD "PhD") in folklore. He is Jewish.

Hirsch was a professor of English at [Wayne State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wayne_State_University "Wayne State University"). In 1985, he joined the faculty at the [University of Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Houston "University of Houston"), where he spent 17 years as a professor in the Creative Writing Program and Department of English. He was appointed the fourth president of the John Simon Guggenheim Foundation on September 3, 2002. He holds seven honorary degrees.

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Edward_Hirsch&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Hirsch is a well-known advocate for poetry whose essays have been published in the _American Poetry Review_, _The New York Times Book Review_, _[The New York Review of Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Review\_of\_Books "The New York Review of Books")_, and elsewhere. He wrote a weekly column on poetry for _The Washington Post Book World_ from 2002 to 2005, which resulted in his book _Poet’s Choice_ (2006). His other prose books include _Responsive Reading_ (1999), _The Demon and the Angel: Searching for the Source of Artistic Inspiration_ (2002), and _A Poet's Glossary_ (2014), a complete compendium of poetic terms. He is the editor of _Transforming Vision: Writers on Art_ (1994), _Theodore Roethke’s Selected Poems_ (2005) and _To a Nightingale_ (2007). He is the co-editor of _A William Maxwell Portrait: Memories and Appreciations_ and _The Making of a Sonnet: A Norton Anthology_ (2008). He also edits the series "The Writer’s World" (Trinity University Press).

Hirsch's first collection of poems, _For the Sleepwalkers_, received the Lavan Younger Poets Award from the Academy of American Poets[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hirsch#cite_note-1) and the Delmore Schwartz Memorial Award from New York University. His second book, _Wild Gratitude_, received the National Book Critics Circle Award in 1986. He was awarded a Guggenheim Fellowship[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hirsch#cite_note-pf-2) in 1985 and a five-year [MacArthur Fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacArthur_Fellowship "MacArthur Fellowship") in 1997. He received the [William Riley Parker Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Riley_Parker_Prize "William Riley Parker Prize") from the Modern Language Association for the best scholarly essay in _PMLA_ for the year 1991. He has also received an [Ingram Merrill Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingram_Merrill_Foundation "Ingram Merrill Foundation") Award, a National Endowment for the Arts Fellowship, the Rome Prize from the American Academy in Rome, a Pablo Neruda Presidential Medal of Honor, and the American Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Literature. He is a former Chancellor of the Academy of American Poets. A volume of his poetry, _Earthly Measures_, was selected by critic Harold Bloom for inclusion on his list of works defining the [Western Canon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Western_Canon "The Western Canon").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Hirsch#cite_note-3) Hirsch's book _How to Read a Poem and Fall in Love with Poetry_ (1999) was a surprise bestseller and is widely taught throughout the country.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American independent, non-profit publisher

Graywolf Press[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/77/Graywolf_Press_Logo.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Graywolf_Press_Logo.png)
Founded 1974
Founders Scott Walker and Kathleen Foster
Successor Carmen Giménez
Country of origin United States
Headquarters location[Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis,_Minnesota "Minneapolis, Minnesota"), [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), U.S.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-history-1)
Distribution[Farrar, Straus and Giroux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrar,_Straus_and_Giroux "Farrar, Straus and Giroux") ([Macmillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macmillan_Publishers "Macmillan Publishers")) (US)  
Turnaround Publisher Services (UK)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-2)
Official website[www.graywolfpress.org](http://www.graywolfpress.org/)

**Graywolf Press** is an [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_publisher "Independent publisher"), [non-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit "Non-profit")[publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishing "Publishing") located in [Minneapolis, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis,_Minnesota "Minneapolis, Minnesota"). Graywolf Press publishes [fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiction "Fiction"), [non-fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction "Non-fiction"), and [poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry "Poetry").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-history-1)

Graywolf Press collaborates with organizations such as the [College of Saint Benedict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Saint_Benedict "College of Saint Benedict"), the [Mellon Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellon_Foundation "Mellon Foundation"), and [Farrar, Straus and Giroux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrar,_Straus_and_Giroux "Farrar, Straus and Giroux").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-history-1)

Graywolf Press currently publishes about 27 books a year, including the Graywolf Press Nonfiction Prize winner, the recipient of the Emily Dickinson First Book Award, and several translations supported by the [Lannan Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lannan_Foundation "Lannan Foundation").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Graywolf_Press&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Graywolf Press was founded by Scott Walker and Kathleen Foster in 1974, in a space provided by [Copper Canyon Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_Canyon_Press "Copper Canyon Press") in [Port Townsend, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Townsend,_Washington "Port Townsend, Washington"). The press was named for the nearby Graywolf Ridge and Graywolf River, and for the [canid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canid "Canid"). The press had early successes publishing poetry heavyweights such as [Denis Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Johnson "Denis Johnson") and [Tess Gallagher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tess_Gallagher "Tess Gallagher").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-4) In 1984, Graywolf Press was incorporated as a [501(c)3 non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit "Non-profit"), and moved to [St. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Paul,_Minnesota "Saint Paul, Minnesota"), [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), in 1985 with the support of the [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts"). Fiona McCrae, formerly of [Faber and Faber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faber_and_Faber "Faber and Faber"), became the director of Graywolf Press in 1994, following the departure of Scott Walker.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-history-1) In 2009, Graywolf Press moved its publishing operations to the historic [Warehouse District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Loop,_Minneapolis "North Loop, Minneapolis") of downtown [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis"), Minnesota. In 2022, [Carmen Giménez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen_Gim%C3%A9nez "Carmen Giménez") became the Executive Director and Publisher.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-5)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Graywolf_Press&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Awards")]

Graywolf Press won the 2015 [AWP Small Press Publisher Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_AWP_Small_Press_Publisher_Award "List of winners of the AWP Small Press Publisher Award") given by the [Association of Writers & Writing Programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Writers_&_Writing_Programs#Small_Press_Publisher_Award "Association of Writers & Writing Programs") that "acknowledges the hard work, creativity, and innovation" of small presses and "their contributions to the literary landscape" of the US.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-7)

## Graywolf Press Prizes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Graywolf_Press&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Graywolf Press Prizes")]

The Graywolf Press Nonfiction Prize, founded in 2005, "seeks to acknowledge – and honor – the great traditions of literary nonfiction” by publishing “the boldest and most innovative books from emerging nonfiction writers" (Robert Polito). Submissions of finished books to the Nonfiction Prize are welcomed from previously unpublished U.S. authors. The winner is announced in April of each year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-8) Graywolf also oversees publication of winners of the [Academy of American Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_American_Poets "Academy of American Poets")' Walt Whitman Award,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-9) as well as every third winner of the Cave Canem Poetry Prize.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-10)

In September 2025, Graywolf Press announced that they were no longer accepting submissions for or awarding the Graywolf Press Nonfiction Prize.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-11)

Since 2018, Graywolf Press has also awarded a prize for "a first novel manuscript by an African author primarily residing in Africa."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-13) The winners include:

### Pegasus Poetry Book Prize

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Graywolf_Press&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Pegasus Poetry Book Prize")]

In November 2025, [Poetry Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Foundation "Poetry Foundation") and Graywolf Press announced a joint prize between the two organizations, with the first prize to be awarded in October 2026.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-16) People eligible to win this prize are "United States poet[s] aged 40 or older for their first or second poetry collection."

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

American independent, non-profit publisher

Graywolf Press[![Image 4](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/7/77/Graywolf_Press_Logo.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Graywolf_Press_Logo.png)
Founded 1974
Founders Scott Walker and Kathleen Foster
Successor Carmen Giménez
Country of origin United States
Headquarters location[Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis,_Minnesota "Minneapolis, Minnesota"), [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), U.S.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-history-1)
Distribution[Farrar, Straus and Giroux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrar,_Straus_and_Giroux "Farrar, Straus and Giroux") ([Macmillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macmillan_Publishers "Macmillan Publishers")) (US)  
Turnaround Publisher Services (UK)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-2)
Official website[www.graywolfpress.org](http://www.graywolfpress.org/)

**Graywolf Press** is an [independent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_publisher "Independent publisher"), [non-profit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit "Non-profit")[publisher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publishing "Publishing") located in [Minneapolis, Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis,_Minnesota "Minneapolis, Minnesota"). Graywolf Press publishes [fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiction "Fiction"), [non-fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction "Non-fiction"), and [poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry "Poetry").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-history-1)

Graywolf Press collaborates with organizations such as the [College of Saint Benedict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Saint_Benedict "College of Saint Benedict"), the [Mellon Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mellon_Foundation "Mellon Foundation"), and [Farrar, Straus and Giroux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farrar,_Straus_and_Giroux "Farrar, Straus and Giroux").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-history-1)

Graywolf Press currently publishes about 27 books a year, including the Graywolf Press Nonfiction Prize winner, the recipient of the Emily Dickinson First Book Award, and several translations supported by the [Lannan Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lannan_Foundation "Lannan Foundation").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-3)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Graywolf_Press&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Graywolf Press was founded by Scott Walker and Kathleen Foster in 1974, in a space provided by [Copper Canyon Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copper_Canyon_Press "Copper Canyon Press") in [Port Townsend, Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_Townsend,_Washington "Port Townsend, Washington"). The press was named for the nearby Graywolf Ridge and Graywolf River, and for the [canid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canid "Canid"). The press had early successes publishing poetry heavyweights such as [Denis Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Johnson "Denis Johnson") and [Tess Gallagher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tess_Gallagher "Tess Gallagher").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-4) In 1984, Graywolf Press was incorporated as a [501(c)3 non-profit organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-profit "Non-profit"), and moved to [St. Paul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Paul,_Minnesota "Saint Paul, Minnesota"), [Minnesota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minnesota "Minnesota"), in 1985 with the support of the [National Endowment for the Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Endowment_for_the_Arts "National Endowment for the Arts"). Fiona McCrae, formerly of [Faber and Faber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faber_and_Faber "Faber and Faber"), became the director of Graywolf Press in 1994, following the departure of Scott Walker.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-history-1) In 2009, Graywolf Press moved its publishing operations to the historic [Warehouse District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Loop,_Minneapolis "North Loop, Minneapolis") of downtown [Minneapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minneapolis "Minneapolis"), Minnesota. In 2022, [Carmen Giménez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmen_Gim%C3%A9nez "Carmen Giménez") became the Executive Director and Publisher.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-5)

## Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Graywolf_Press&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Awards")]

Graywolf Press won the 2015 [AWP Small Press Publisher Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_AWP_Small_Press_Publisher_Award "List of winners of the AWP Small Press Publisher Award") given by the [Association of Writers & Writing Programs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Writers_&_Writing_Programs#Small_Press_Publisher_Award "Association of Writers & Writing Programs") that "acknowledges the hard work, creativity, and innovation" of small presses and "their contributions to the literary landscape" of the US.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-7)

## Graywolf Press Prizes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Graywolf_Press&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Graywolf Press Prizes")]

The Graywolf Press Nonfiction Prize, founded in 2005, "seeks to acknowledge – and honor – the great traditions of literary nonfiction” by publishing “the boldest and most innovative books from emerging nonfiction writers" (Robert Polito). Submissions of finished books to the Nonfiction Prize are welcomed from previously unpublished U.S. authors. The winner is announced in April of each year.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-8) Graywolf also oversees publication of winners of the [Academy of American Poets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_American_Poets "Academy of American Poets")' Walt Whitman Award,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-9) as well as every third winner of the Cave Canem Poetry Prize.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-10)

In September 2025, Graywolf Press announced that they were no longer accepting submissions for or awarding the Graywolf Press Nonfiction Prize.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-11)

### Pegasus Poetry Book Prize

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Graywolf_Press&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Pegasus Poetry Book Prize")]

In November 2025, [Poetry Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poetry_Foundation "Poetry Foundation") and Graywolf Press announced a joint prize between the two organizations, with the first prize to be awarded in October 2026.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graywolf_Press#cite_note-16) People eligible to win this prize are "United States poet[s] aged 40 or older for their first or second poetry collection."

# Pegasus Poetry Book Prize

Share

The Pegasus Poetry Book Prize, established in 2025 in partnership with Graywolf Press, awards $10,000 and publication to an unpublished first or second poetry collection by a United States poet 40 or older. The recipient will also receive a residency at Ragdale. This prize replaces the Poetry Foundation’s former [Emily Dickinson First Book Award](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/awards/past-awards) and will be offered periodically rather than annually.

2026 Pegasus Poetry Book Prize Recipient

*   ![Image 6: meg-day](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=10,h=10,q=50,blur=3/content/images/pol/2021-08/meg-day.jpeg)2026 Sound Lasso By Meg Day  [Meg Day](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/meg-day)’s second full-length collection, _Sound Lasso_, captures the many ways we can “sing without a sound.” In Day’s poems, desires of the mind and body echo with divine potential. The book traces absent lovers through a series of [aubades](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/education/glossary/aubade), reconceives the self in various portraits, and offers Deaf [erasures](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/education/glossary/erasure-poetry) that suggest the inaudible can be both blessing and comfort as we find new ways of speaking. This lush, searching book reminds us that naming—ourselves, each other, and our various hungers—can be a powerful improvisation, akin to godliness.

–Lindsay Garbutt, deputy editor, _Poetry_

_Sound Lasso_ will be published by Graywolf Press in 2028.

**Finalist**

The 2026 finalist for the Pegasus Poetry Book Prize was _The Far Edge of the Wound Is a Field,_ a manuscript by[Paul Hlava Ceballos](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/paul-hlava-ceballos).

# Pegasus Poetry Book Prize

Share

The Pegasus Poetry Book Prize, established in 2025 in partnership with Graywolf Press, awards $10,000 and publication to an unpublished first or second poetry collection by a United States poet 40 or older. The recipient will also receive a residency at Ragdale. This prize replaces the Poetry Foundation’s former [Emily Dickinson First Book Award](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/awards/past-awards) and will be offered periodically rather than annually.

2026 Pegasus Poetry Book Prize Recipient

*   ![Image 6: meg-day](https://cdn.poetryfoundation.org/cdn-cgi/image/w=10,h=10,q=50,blur=3/content/images/pol/2021-08/meg-day.jpeg)2026 Sound Lasso By Meg Day  [Meg Day](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/meg-day)’s second full-length collection, _Sound Lasso_, captures the many ways we can “sing without a sound.” In Day’s poems, desires of the mind and body echo with divine potential. The book traces absent lovers through a series of [aubades](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/education/glossary/aubade), reconceives the self in various portraits, and offers Deaf [erasures](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/education/glossary/erasure-poetry) that suggest the inaudible can be both blessing and comfort as we find new ways of speaking. This lush, searching book reminds us that naming—ourselves, each other, and our various hungers—can be a powerful improvisation, akin to godliness.

–Lindsay Garbutt, deputy editor, _Poetry_

_Sound Lasso_ will be published by Graywolf Press in 2028.

**Finalist**

The 2026 finalist for the Pegasus Poetry Book Prize was _The Far Edge of the Wound Is a Field,_ a manuscript by[Paul Hlava Ceballos](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/paul-hlava-ceballos).

# Past Awards

*   [Current Poetry Foundation Awards](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/awards)

These awards are not currently active. For updates on Poetry Foundation offerings, including awards, please subscribe to [our newsletter](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/newsletter).

## Emily Dickinson First Book Award

The Emily Dickinson First Book Award is designed to recognize an American poet of at least 40 years of age who has yet to publish a first collection of poetry. The most recent recipient of this award was [Kristen Tracy](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/kristen-tracy) in [2017 for her collection _Half-Hazard_](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/articles/142163/poetry-foundation-announces-kristen-tracy-winner-of-2017-emily-dickinson-first-book-award).

## Randall Jarrell Award in Criticism

The Randall Jarrell Award in Criticism recognized poetry criticism aimed at a large general readership rather than an audience of specialists.

## Mark Twain Poetry Award

**Echo Echo** is [Carbon Leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Leaf "Carbon Leaf")'s fourth album. It was released in 2001 by the band's own label, Constant Ivy Records.

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Echo_Echo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Release")]

"The Boxer" went on to bring Carbon Leaf local, regional, and even some national recognition. In January 2002 Carbon Leaf won the first-ever [American Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Music_Award "American Music Award") Presents the Coca-Cola New Music Award for "The Boxer."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echo_Echo#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echo_Echo#cite_note-5) As part of winning they performed "The Boxer" live on the AMAs to 80 million television viewers worldwide. Following this appearance, "The Boxer" entered regular rotation on radio stations including [Washington, DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_DC "Washington, DC")'s DC101 ([WWDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWDC_(FM) "WWDC (FM)") 101.1 FM).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

**Echo Echo** is [Carbon Leaf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carbon_Leaf "Carbon Leaf")'s fourth album. It was released in 2001 by the band's own label, Constant Ivy Records.

## Release

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Echo_Echo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Release")]

"The Boxer" went on to bring Carbon Leaf local, regional, and even some national recognition. In January 2002 Carbon Leaf won the first-ever [American Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Music_Award "American Music Award") Presents the Coca-Cola New Music Award for "The Boxer."[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echo_Echo#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Echo_Echo#cite_note-5) As part of winning they performed "The Boxer" live on the AMAs to 80 million television viewers worldwide. Following this appearance, "The Boxer" entered regular rotation on radio stations including [Washington, DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_DC "Washington, DC")'s DC101 ([WWDC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WWDC_(FM) "WWDC (FM)") 101.1 FM).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
